name: Colorado Midland Railway
basis: East of Divide the line is one continuous route of 26.82 miles to Colorado Springs, from a tracing supplied by the atlas's owner and tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 83 per cent of it lies on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent, and each mile carries its own grade and error (see atlas/tools/once_route_cm_east.py). The Midland Terminal's timetables give 26.9 miles for the same run. Through the tunnel district above Manitou, 17 to 20 miles from Divide, the test reads poorly because of the tunnels themselves; seven tunnel points marked on a supplied map all lie within about 120 ft of the route there. West of Divide the line is one continuous route of 13.47 miles through Florissant to the edge of the region, from the line 'Divide to Leadville' in a Google Earth file supplied by the owner, tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 92 per cent on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent (see atlas/tools/once_route_cm_west.py). About a mile and a half near its west end has no lidar held and is untested. Beyond the atlas's first region the line runs on west through Leadville and Glenwood Springs to New Castle, with the Aspen, Spring Gulch and Leadville branches, the Aspen Short Line and the Busk-Ivanhoe tunnel: 239.0 miles of traced lines from a Google Earth file supplied by the owner, whose maker is not recorded (share on a smooth lidar grade: not yet tested). Marked inferred, about 150 ft, and untested. Added up from Colorado Springs the main line comes to about 232 miles, against 233.91 in Poor's Manual of 1892 and 233.5 in the timetable of October 1888.
notes: From Poor's manuals: chartered 23 November 1883; construction begun April 1886 and 100 miles completed by 1 July 1887, which covers the line up Ute Pass; road opened throughout 15 October 1888; receivers appointed 1 February 1894; sold under foreclosure 8 September 1897 and succeeded by the Colorado Midland Railway, chartered 11 October 1897. The end is still from secondary sources, which disagree: operations stopped in August 1918, the line was abandoned in 1921 and the company dissolved in 1922. East of Divide the track passed to the Midland Terminal: its timetable of 7 September 1920 already runs from Colorado Springs. Those segments are dated to 1949.

name: Colorado Springs and Cripple Creek District Railway (the Short Line)
basis: From the edge of Colorado Springs to Cameron the line is one continuous route of 36.97 miles, tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 90 per cent of what could be tested lies on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent, and each mile carries its own grade and error (see atlas/tools/once_route_shortline.py). It is the OpenStreetMap pieces put in order, with two gaps (1.1 and 6.2 miles) followed along Gold Camp Road, which runs on the grade. Against the timetable of 26 September 1909, Duffields, Rosemont and Cameron Junction each fall 2.9 to 3.0 miles later on the route than their printed miles from Colorado Springs Yard, so the route's length agrees with the timetable to a tenth of a mile over 21 miles, and it begins about 3 miles out from the yard (that first stretch is the next route). name: Midland Terminal Railway
basis: From Divide to the end of the surviving trace near Independence the line is one continuous route of 21.7 miles, tested against the 1 m lidar mile by mile: 94 per cent of it lies on smooth ground under 4.5 per cent, and each mile carries its own grade and error (see atlas/tools/once_route_mt.py). It is the OpenStreetMap pieces put in order, with two gaps between Divide and Midland crossed by a line found from the lidar. The timetables put Gillett 14.4 and Cameron 19.7 miles from Divide; the route puts them at 14.6 and 19.8. Beyond Independence the line goes on by the routes below. An OpenStreetMap piece running 2.85 miles south-west from Gillett, once shown as part of this line, is removed: the USGS district map of 1903 draws no railway there and it follows the present Highway 67. Between Cripple Creek and Victor (by Anaconda, Beacon Hill, Elkton and Eclipse) the line is a trace of 4.75 miles from the USGS district map surveyed in 1894 and revised in 1902-1903 (Professional Paper 54, plate 1), inferred and good to about 200 ft at best: only 1 per cent of it reads as a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar, because most of that ground is now the open-pit mine. The timetable of 1920 gives 5.3 miles for the same run. Where the map draws several railways side by side the trace is not told apart from the Florence and Cripple Creek's (see atlas/tools/once_route_district.py). Into Victor the upper of the map's two lines is taken as this railway's: the key maps of the Sanborn sheets of August 1900 and December 1908 letter the upper line Midland Terminal, with a switchback, and the lower Florence and Cripple Creek. It now stops west of Victor, where it nears a bench that survives on the foot of Squaw Mountain; that bench carries the line to Victor Junction and the depot leg (the map's line lay up to 150 m from the bench there). Below Independence the line is carried 1.87 miles toward Victor (26 per cent of it on a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar, all of that in the first half mile). The first half mile, a horseshoe, is a surviving bench that the Divide route meets within 2 m, and the USGS map surveyed in 1894 letters the Midland Terminal on a line of that shape: bench measured, attribution inferred. Beyond it, along the east foot of Battle Mountain and west past the Portland mine, only the corridor is drawn, good to about 300 ft: the 1903 map has three to five unnamed tracks side by side there and the ground is reworked. The descent into Victor goes on in the next route (see atlas/tools/once_route_mt_victor_side.py and once_route_victor_sanborn.py). Through Victor the line is 0.78 miles of pieces taken from the Sanborn fire insurance sheets of December 1908 (sheets 2 and 3, fitted to the present street corners to 2 to 4 m RMS), with the 1903 map above the town (42 per cent smooth on the 1 m lidar, weighted by length). The sheets of 1896, 1900 and 1908 agree: the main track passes the north-west corner of the town, and the depot at 4th Street and Granite Avenue stands on a leg lettered 'Switchback', entered by reversing (Moody's of 1917 describes a branch to Victor). The main track past the town and the track by the depot lie on surviving smooth ground and are measured; the leg is inferred, good to about 25 ft. Where the leg left the main track is not on any sheet read; it was found on the lidar west of the town (next route). Above the town, from the rim of the open pit down, the line follows the 1903 map through ground the pit and its dumps have replaced (see atlas/tools/once_route_victor_sanborn.py). West of the town the main track and the depot leg are carried 0.77 miles on two benches that survive on the south-west foot of Squaw Mountain (83 per cent smooth on the 1 m lidar, weighted by length; the two benches themselves read 100 per cent). The main track falls westward from 3,015 to 3,004 m and the leg climbs westward from 2,990 to 3,002 m; they meet at a sharp angle 400 m west of the leg's end on the Sanborn sheet, so the depot was reached by running past and backing down. By the drawn line that meeting point is 0.56 mile from the depot, and the timetables of 1920 and 1932 print Victor Junction 0.6 mile from Victor: it is taken to be Victor Junction, and replaces a join that was marked conjecture. The 'Switchback' of the 1920 timetable is a different place, 1.1 miles before Victor on the Independence side, not located. West of the junction one bench is followed a fifth of a mile toward Eclipse, poorly (see atlas/tools/once_route_victor_joins.py).
notes: Incorporated 9 August 1892 under Colorado laws; 29.4 miles from Divide to Cripple Creek with a branch to Victor; controlled by the Cripple Creek Central from 1904 (Moody's 1917). The timetable of 14 July 1895 runs Divide, Gillett, Grassy, Independence, Victor, with a stage from Grassy to Cripple Creek; by the table of 26 September 1909 Cripple Creek is a station at 30 miles. From 1920 the tables run from Colorado Springs; from January 1945 they are marked freight service only; the last read is March 1948. Still from secondary sources: rails to Midland in December 1893 and Gillett on 4 July 1894, into Cripple Creek in December 1895, last run February 1949. The drawn line is dated from 1894.

name: Florence and Cripple Creek Railroad
basis: Between Cripple Creek and Victor the line is a trace of 4.77 miles from the USGS district map surveyed in 1894 and revised in 1902-1903 (Professional Paper 54, plate 1), inferred: 15 per cent of it reads as a smooth grade on the 1 m lidar. For about a mile south of Cripple Creek it is laid on the bench the tourist railway now uses, which the map's line follows at a typical 45 m; the rest is good to about 200 ft at best and lies mostly in ground now mined. The timetable of 2 June 1895 gives 5.7 miles from Cripple Creek to Victor. Where the map draws several railways side by side the trace is not told apart from the Midland Terminal's (see atlas/tools/once_route_district.py). It now stops where it reaches Victor; the Sanborn sheets carry it through the town. South of Victor the line to Florence is not traced; two tunnels in Phantom Canyon are from OpenStreetMap. Through Victor the line is 0.45 miles from the Sanborn sheets of December 1908 (sheets 2 and 3; 58 per cent smooth on the 1 m lidar, weighted by length): from west of 7th Street east along the south side of Diamond Avenue, across 4th Street and north-east past its own frame depot west of 3rd Street, then east between Granite and Diamond Avenues. Good to about 15 to 25 ft in the town; the short join to the 1903 trace west of the town is inferred (see atlas/tools/once_route_victor_sanborn.py). East of the Sanborn sheet the line is carried 0.74 miles to Phantom Canyon Road (85 per cent of it smooth, nearly level ground on the 1 m lidar). The USGS district map of 1903 draws the railway leaving its yard eastward, turning through a hairpin and going south; that map lies 150 to 200 m off on this side, so the line is laid on banks and a road curve on the lidar that match its shape. Inferred, good to about 300 ft, and not confirmed by any large-scale map (see atlas/tools/once_route_victor_joins.py). Through Phantom Canyon the line is one continuous route of 27.81 miles, from where the old grade from Florence runs into Phantom Canyon Road (1.4 miles north of US 50) to the edge of Victor (its last 0.15 mile, where the road cuts a corner, is taken off), following the road, which by all accounts (secondary) is built on the railway's bed: 89 per cent of the road from US 50 lies on a smooth, gently graded bench on the 1 m lidar, and the two tunnels already in the atlas lie on it. Marked inferred throughout, since the test shows a graded bench under the road and not who made it (see atlas/tools/once_route_fcc.py). The road's first 1.4 miles north of US 50, shown at first as part of this route, are a section-line road and were cut off: the USGS sheets of 1959 and the lidar put the railway up to a third of a mile west of it there. From Florence to the canyon road the line is 5.35 miles (82 per cent smooth on the 1 m lidar, weighted by length). Its northern 3.6 miles are an embankment that still stands across the open mesa, read off the lidar and lettered 'OLD RAILROAD GRADE' on the USGS sheets of 1959: about 80 per cent of it tests as a smooth grade, the breaks being where gullies have cut through it. At Florence the track through the railway's own ground (round house, and an 'Old R.R. Depot' used as a warehouse by then) is from the Sanborn sheet of September 1906, fitted to four present street corners to about 5 m; north of it to the river the line follows a straight ditch and field edge that continues the Sanborn track's bearing, inferred. The bridge over the Arkansas and the 0.7 mile north of it are not located: that piece is drawn straight and is conjecture. Yard to the Victor depot comes to 34.0 miles by these routes against the 34.6 of the timetable of 2 June 1895 (35.0 in that of 1907); the timetable's Florence was probably the Denver and Rio Grande station east of the yard (not located), which may account for part of the difference (see atlas/tools/once_route_fcc_florence.py). A branch of 1.26 miles leaves the main line 1.1 miles north of the Arkansas and climbs east to the top of the bluff above Florence (99 per cent smooth on the 1 m lidar; lettered 'OLD RR GRADE' on the USGS Florence sheet of 1959). That it served the reduction works is inferred from Poor's Manual of 1899, which lists a branch from Cyanide Junction to Vesta, 1.5 miles; no map read names it.
notes: Narrow gauge (3 ft). Poor's 1895 gives incorporation on 11 May 1893; Poor's 1899 says chartered 10 May 1893 and road opened 1 September 1894; Florence to Cripple Creek 40.3 miles. Moody's 1917: dissolved 1 May 1915, its assets conveyed to the Golden Circle Railroad, renamed the Cripple Creek and Colorado Springs. Secondary sources give other days (first train into Cripple Creek 1 July 1894; dissolved 27 April 1915) and the flood of 21 July 1912 that wrecked the canyon line; the drawn tunnels are dated to 1912 on that account.

name: New Castle to Grand Junction (Denver and Rio Grande, and the Rio Grande Junction Railway): the line the Colorado Midland ran over
basis: Today's track from OpenStreetMap, followed from New Castle to Grand Junction: 75.22 miles, against 75.49 in Poor's Manual of 1892 (13.41 and 62.08), and joining the Colorado Midland's own line at New Castle within 10 ft (share on a smooth lidar grade: not yet tested). It stands in for the line of 1890: realignments since then have not been looked into, so it is inferred, about 200 ft.
railway: Denver and Rio Grande; Rio Grande Junction Railway (leased jointly)
notes: Not the Colorado Midland's own line. Poor's Manual of 1892 lists as leased: the Denver and Rio Grande from New Castle to Rifle, 13.41 miles, and the Rio Grande Junction Railroad from Rifle to Grand Junction, 62.08 miles, and says the Colorado Midland was 'opened to Grand Junction via the Rio Grande Junction RR. on November 16, 1890'. Shown here for the years the Colorado Midland used it, 1890 to about 1918 (the end date is secondary). The railway itself is still in use.
